problem: Diffusion policies for RGB image-goal visual navigation (e.g., NoMaD) sample waypoints that can be unreliable or inefficient. Test-time task guidance (e.g., collision or short-path gradients) pushes reverse-diffusion updates off the training manifold. In addition, the K sampled candidates are usually picked at random or by hand-tuned heuristics rather than by a principled uncertainty measure.
motivation: Diffusion samplers already produce diverse, multi-modal action candidates and carry a rich sensitivity/uncertainty structure, but this structure is rarely used. Sampling guided only by a task loss tends to produce out-of-distribution waypoints, and exact Fisher/Jacobian constraints are too expensive for real-time robot control. The paper's view is that a guided update should keep a Fisher-style sensitivity of the denoiser constant (move along a Fisher isosurface), and that this constraint can be approximated cheaply through the low-rank final linear head.
key_idea: Project each test-time guidance gradient onto the tangent space of a Fisher-sensitivity isosurface, approximated cheaply in the low-rank subspace spanned by the denoiser's final linear head (Outer Product Span), and fuse the K sampled trajectories with weights built from truncated Fisher denoising sensitivity and DBSCAN cluster typicality.
insight: The two inference-time modules have complementary roles in the CARLA ablation. FPG alone raises SR from 48.89 to 64.44 but also raises collisions from 0.700 to 0.911. Action blending alone gives SR 57.78 and the lowest single-module collisions (0.622). Together they reach SR 75.55 with 0.445 collisions and SPL 0.653, while random blending on top of FPG drops back to 57.78 SR and 0.800 collisions, so the TFDS/typicality weighting matters and not averaging per se. The paper's own base model without either module (48.89 SR) is below both NoMaD (51.11) and ViNT (53.33), which indicates the gains come from the training-free inference modules rather than a stronger backbone. The OPS approximation also makes the method cheap: 45.12 ms total at 4 steps, versus 54.81 ms for exact VJP-Fisher and 55.00 ms for 10-step NoMaD on an RTX 3060.
method: Step Fisher Denoising Sensitivity (FDS): I(C,t) = ((1-ᾱ_t)/ᾱ_t)·||∇_C ε_θ(C,a_t,t)||_F², the squared Frobenius norm of the Jacobian of the one-step reconstructed action w.r.t. the observation/goal context C; a proxy for sensitivity of the action to observation perturbations.

Chain FDS and Truncated FDS (TFDS): the chain-rule Jacobian through all T reverse steps (normalized propagation operator, Hutchinson estimator) is replaced by an additive surrogate that keeps only the last M steps. The relative error is bounded by η_M ≤ κ·Σ_{t>M} w_t / Σ_{t≤M} w_t, e.g. η_4 ≤ 8.4% for M=4, T=10, κ≈1. Default M=4.

Fisher-Preserving Guidance (FPG): the task gradient u_t = ∇_{a_t}L has its component along the Fisher normal g_t = ∇_{a_t} I_t(a_t;C) removed, Δ_t = u_t − (u_tᵀg_t/||g_t||²) g_t. The update a_{t−1} = μ_t − γΔ_t then keeps FDS constant to first order, with O(γ²) drift, and is shown to be the steepest first-order descent direction under that constraint.

Outer Product Span (OPS) low-rank approximation: writing ε_θ ≈ W h_θ gives u_h = Wᵀu_t. The Fisher-aligned component is removed under the pullback metric M = WᵀW using a latent Fisher-normal proxy g_h, which comes from the same single backward pass that also yields the condition gradient reused for FDS, and the result is mapped back as Δ_t = W u_h^⊥. This avoids second-order differentiation, at O(C_hH) cost per step.
Uncertainty-guided action blending: K=4 candidates are clustered with DBSCAN (ε=0.5). Each candidate gets weight exp(−η·TFDS)·(cluster size/K), and the final action is the weighted average a_blend.

Base navigation policy: EfficientNet-B0 visual encoder with sparse attention and temporal-shift spatio-temporal fusion (adapted from STRNet), 96×96 images, 3-frame history plus goal image, and a diffusion head predicting an 8-step waypoint horizon plus temporal distance. Trained with the NoMaD objective; subgoal images are switched by predicted temporal distance (ViNT protocol).

Plug-and-play use: FPG and blending are also attached to NoMaD (CARLA), to the official Diffusion Policy weights (PushT) and to a custom DDPM planner with TSDF-barrier task guidance (Maze2D), all without retraining.

setting.backbone: EfficientNet-B0 + sparse-attention/temporal-shift fusion + conditional diffusion policy head (trained from scratch, NoMaD objective); FPG/blending applied training-free at inference. Also applied to NoMaD, to official Diffusion Policy (PushT) and to a ResNet-18 + 1D U-Net DDPM (Maze2D).
setting.training_data: Unified navigation dataset shared by all methods: RECON, SCAND, GoStanford, SACSoN (30 epochs, 4 warmup epochs, batch 256, lr 1e-4). FPG-OPS and blending add no training. Maze2D uses synthetic 64×64 grids with expert trajectories from classical planning on inflated obstacles; PushT uses the official Diffusion Policy checkpoint.

Inconsistencies:
- CARLA SR granularity (e.g., 73.33% = 11/15 per scenario) conflicts with the stated 10 repeats per route.
- The text says 4 DDIM steps by default, but the hyperparameter table lists 10 diffusion steps.
- The blending temperature is called η in the text and β in the hyperparameter table.
results: On 9 CARLA routes, the full method reaches SR 75.55%, 0.445 collisions and SPL 0.653, compared with ViNT (53.33 / 0.611 / 0.504) and NoMaD (51.11 / 0.778 / 0.478). Adding FPG or blending alone to NoMaD also helps (60.00 and 57.78 SR). On GRScenes in Isaac Sim, it reaches SR 83.0, 0.48 collisions and SPL 0.83, compared with ViNT at 68.0 / 0.71 / 0.77. On a real Diablo robot it succeeds in 28/30 runs with 0.10 collisions (ViNT 22/30, NoMaD 19/30). FPG also lowers Maze2D collision with TSDF guidance from 0.071 to 0.016 and raises the PushT score from 0.91 to 0.94. With 4 steps it is faster than NoMaD (45.12 vs 55.00 ms).
limitations: FDS/TFDS is only a heuristic Fisher-style sensitivity proxy with no certified safety guarantee. The OPS normal proxy g_h and the navigation task loss L are only loosely specified.

Evaluation uses small custom route sets (9 CARLA routes, 10 GRScenes routes, 30 real trials) rather than standard benchmarks, with no confidence intervals and some protocol inconsistencies (trial counts, 4 vs 10 diffusion steps).

The headline comparison mixes a different base model (STRNet-style) with the inference modules. Only the NoMaD+FPG and NoMaD+Blending rows isolate the plug-in effect, and those gains are modest (+8.9 and +6.7 SR).
